passage: The storm knocked out the office internet at two, and the client email was due by five. Jyoti opened her assistant out of habit and got only a grey error. Her stomach dipped. Every email and every idea for the last year had started there. She stared at the blank message for ten minutes, then wrote two clumsy sentences, deleted them and wrote again. Rehana, at the next desk, slid over a mug of tea and read the draft aloud. "The second line is yours, isn't it? It sounds like you." By half past four Jyoti had a rough draft, and it was hers. When the internet returned, she asked the assistant to tighten it, then checked each date it changed. She kept the habit: first draft by hand, help after.

qa.q: What knocked out the office internet?
qa.a: The storm knocked out the office internet.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when the assistant showed only a grey error?
qa.a: Her stomach dipped. She felt uneasy, seeing that every email and idea of the last year had started with the assistant.

qa.q: What habit did Jyoti adopt, and why is it a sound one?
qa.a: She writes the first draft herself and asks for help after, checking what the assistant changes. That keeps her own skills sharp while still using the convenience.

qa.q: What might Rehana notice in Jyoti's draft?
qa.a: Rehana heard Jyoti's own voice in the second line, which suggests the writing still had a personal touch worth keeping.

grounding: Using AI for every email and idea makes skills fade; a forced offline afternoon leads to drafting first herself and then checking the tool's changes.

passage:
Aadhya's diary. Wednesday. A bit rattled.

Today Harsha asked me, in the team meeting, what I actually thought about the new client's brief. Not the chatbot. Me.

And I froze. For months I've let the AI assistant write every email, every idea list, even my birthday message to Papa. I opened my mouth and nothing organised came out.

Harsha was kind about it afterwards. "You used to have the best ideas in the room," Harsha said. "Where did they go?"

I think they went into the prompt box.

So, new rule, starting tomorrow: I write the first draft myself, badly if I have to, and only then ask the tool to tidy it. I check anything it claims. One day a week, no AI at all.

Tonight I wrote this entry by hand. It took forty minutes. My handwriting is awful, but these are my own sentences.

qa.q: How long did Aadhya's handwritten entry take?
How did Aadhya feel when Harsha asked for an opinion in the meeting?
qa.a: Aadhya felt rattled and embarrassed, freezing because the ideas were no longer organised in their own words.

qa.q: What would you say about Aadhya's new rule?
qa.a: It keeps the tool as a collaborator: drafting first, checking its claims, and one AI-free day a week will help rebuild Aadhya's own skills.

qa.q: How does Harsha see the change in Aadhya?
qa.a: Harsha seems concerned and a little sad, remembering Aadhya once had the best ideas in the room.

grounding: The diary shows someone who uses AI for every email and idea and notices their own skills fading, and decides to draft first themselves and check the tool's claims.

passage:
Bhavna: Manoj, can I ask something weird
Manoj: always
Bhavna: my colleague's father died. I've been trying to write her a message for an hour
Bhavna: I asked the AI and it gave me something perfect but it doesn't sound like me at all
Bhavna: and I realised I don't know how to write it without it
Manoj: that's not weird. that's honest
Manoj: forget perfect. what do you actually want her to know
Bhavna: that I'm sorry. that she doesn't have to reply. that I remember her dad dropping her at office on Fridays
Manoj: that's the message. write exactly that
Bhavna: it's so plain
Manoj: plain is how people who care sound 🤍
Bhavna: ok. sending
Bhavna: sent. I'm going to start writing my own stuff first again. I've got rusty
Manoj: rusty isn't gone

qa.q: What does Bhavna remember about the colleague's father?
qa.a: Him dropping her at the office on Fridays.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when she realised she couldn't write the message without AI?
qa.a: Bhavna felt uneasy and a little ashamed, worried that Bhavna's own writing skills had faded.

qa.q: What did Manoj advise, and why did it work?
qa.a: Manoj asked what Bhavna actually wanted the colleague to know and said to write exactly that, which gave a plain, personal message instead of a polished one.

qa.q: How might Bhavna's colleague receive the plain message?
qa.a: The colleague may feel comforted by a personal detail about her father that no tool could have known.

grounding: The chat shows someone who has leaned on AI for every message noticing their own skills fading, and deciding to draft in their own words first.
